# Should I Avoid Temptation?

> "For God didn't give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control."
>
> — 2 Timothy 1:7

Up to now this book has given orders: carry on as normal until the end, no cutting down, no substitutes. Each has a solid reason behind it.

This chapter is different. On avoiding temptation I can't hand you a rule, because the answer depends on your life. You'll have to judge for yourself, and I can only help you judge well.

What keeps a man jerking off for life is fear of what life would be like without it. That fear comes in two phases.

## Phase One: "How will I get through tonight?" {-}

This is the panic. It comes when the evening stretches ahead with nobody in it, when your wife is away or you haven't got one.

The panic is not a withdrawal pang. It's the belief that you can't cope without your release. It's strongest just before you stop, when your body is asking for nothing at all. It is plain fear of the unknown, the same thing a boy feels on his first diving board.

The board is two feet above the water, and from up there it looks like twenty. The pool is ten feet deep and looks like a puddle. Every instinct tells him he's about to crack his skull. Stepping off takes real nerve. After that the rest is easy, and he comes up laughing.

This is why men of obvious courage have never once tried to stop, and why others last three days. It's even why some men go on a binge the very day they decide to quit. The decision sets off the panic, panic is a cue, and now the comfort is "forbidden", so the pressure climbs until the fuse goes.

Don't worry. The panic is in your head, and the beautiful truth is that you don't depend on the thing, even now, while you're still in the trap. Paul says the spirit God gives is not one of fear. If you're an atheist, play along: the water's deep enough, and plenty of men have jumped before you.

DON'T PANIC. STEP OFF THE BOARD.

## Phase Two: "What about the rest of my life?" {-}

The second fear is slower. It's the worry that some future situation won't be bearable without the habit: the lonely Christmas, the months when your wife is ill, a bereavement. Step off the board and you'll find the opposite is true, as Chapter 23 explained.

That leaves the practical question, which comes in two forms.

## "Should I keep a way back, just in case?" {-}

Some men stop but keep an escape hatch: the saved folder, the account they still follow "for the workouts", or a private rule that says, "If it gets really bad I'm allowed one."

They think the hatch makes them braver. It does the reverse. Men who keep a way back fail far more often than men who close the door. When a bad moment comes, using the hatch costs nothing, because the excuse was written in advance. A man who'd have to smash his own word will usually wait, and while he waits the urge passes.

But the main reason these men fail is that they were never fully committed. The two essentials are:

1. **Certainty.**
2. **"Isn't it marvellous that I don't need it any more?"**

So what's the hatch *for*? If you still want one, something hasn't clicked. Re-read the book and kill the Big Monster properly.

## The phone in the bedroom {-}

"Should I get the phone out of my bedroom? Or is that running scared?"

There are two opposite mistakes.

**The first is the fortress.** This man bans the internet, avoids the beach, and looks at his shoes when a woman walks past. Every change tells him the same thing: "I'm in terrible danger and I've given up a great deal." That's the Willpower Method with a fence round it.

**The second is the dare.** This man lies in bed at midnight with the phone on his chest to prove how strong he is. He's being a fool. Testing yourself adds nothing to your freedom. John Piper's advice is common sense: "Be vigilant over your eyes. Avoid unnecessary stimulation." The word to notice is *unnecessary*.

So charge the phone in the kitchen. Do it because bed is a stupid place for a phone at midnight, whatever you look at. You're not doing it because you're in danger. Unfollow the accounts you followed for one reason. Delete the folder. Then stop rearranging your life.

Joseph shows you both halves. When Potiphar's wife caught him by his coat, he "ran outside". He didn't stay to test his character. But he hadn't been hiding from the house either. He'd gone in that day to do his work.

FLEE WHAT'S STUPID. LIVE THE REST NORMALLY.

## "Should I stay in for a few weeks?" {-}

If you mean needless *stress*, then yes, within reason. You don't have to prove anything.

If you mean your social life, the advice is the opposite. Go out straight away, to the wedding, the party, the beach. Talk to women and look them in the eye. FitXFearless gives the same advice to men who want to stay free: "be social go out go to events go to brunch go to parties".

What sent you back to your room in the past was mostly an empty evening, so fill your evenings with people. And enjoy this while you're out: you don't *need* anything from any woman in the room. You can talk to her, like her and go home with a clear head. That's self-control with the fear gone out of it, and Paul puts it in the same breath as power and love. A man who can't control his lust can't be trusted, and you're turning into a man who can be.

If it's this good while the Little Monster is still twitching, think what it'll be like when he's gone.
